Miriam's and Aaron's Sedition.</title> <div sID="gen1820" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1348"/><hi type="bold">1. an Ethiopian woman--</hi>Hebrew, "a Cushite woman"--Arabia was usually called in Scripture the land of Cush, its inhabitants being descendants of that son of Ham (see on <reference osisRef="Exod.2.15">Ex 2:15</reference>) and being accounted generally a vile and contemptible race (see on <reference osisRef="Amos.9.7">Am 9:7</reference>). The occasion of this seditious outbreak on the part of Miriam and Aaron against Moses was the great change made in the government by the adoption of the seventy rulers [Nu 11:16]. Their irritating disparagement of his wife (who, in all probability, was Zipporah [Ex 2:21], and not a second wife he had recently married) arose from jealousy of the relatives, through whose influence the innovation had been first made (<reference osisRef="Exod.18.13-Exod.18.26">Ex 18:13-26</reference>), while they were overlooked or neglected. Miriam is mentioned before Aaron as being the chief instigator and leader of the sedition. <div eID="gen1820" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain:
CHAPTER 12
 
Nu 12:1-9. Miriam's and Aaron's Sedition.

1. an Ethiopian woman--Hebrew, "a Cushite woman"--Arabia was usually called in Scripture the land of Cush, its inhabitants being descendants of that son of Ham (see on Ex 2:15) and being accounted generally a vile and contemptible race (see on Am 9:7). The occasion of this seditious outbreak on the part of Miriam and Aaron against Moses was the great change made in the government by the adoption of the seventy rulers [Nu 11:16]. Their irritating disparagement of his wife (who, in all probability, was Zipporah [Ex 2:21], and not a second wife he had recently married) arose from jealousy of the relatives, through whose influence the innovation had been first made (Ex 18:13-26), while they were overlooked or neglected. Miriam is mentioned before Aaron as being the chief instigator and leader of the sedition.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1350"/><div sID="gen1822" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1350"/><hi type="bold">3. the man Moses was very meek--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Exod.14.13">Ex 14:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.32.12">32:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.13">13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.14.13">Nu 14:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.21.7">21:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.9.18">De 9:18</reference>). This observation might have been made to account for Moses taking no notice of their angry reproaches and for God's interposing so speedily for the vindication of His servant's cause. The circumstance of Moses recording an eulogium on a distinguishing excellence of his own character is not without a parallel among the sacred writers, when forced to it by the insolence and contempt of opponents (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.5">2Co 11:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.11">12:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.12">12</reference>). But it is not improbable that, as this verse appears to be a parenthesis, it may have been inserted as a gloss by Ezra or some later prophet. Others, instead of "very meek," suggest "very afflicted," as the proper rendering. <div eID="gen1822" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1353"/><div sID="gen1825" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1353"/><hi type="bold">6-7. Hear now my words--</hi>A difference of degree is here distinctly expressed in the gifts and authority even of divinely commissioned prophets. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1354"/><div sID="gen1826" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1354"/><hi type="bold">8. with him will I speak mouth to mouth--</hi>immediately, not by an interpreter, nor by visionary symbols presented to his fancy.<div eID="gen1826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1827" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">apparently--</hi>plainly and surely.<div eID="gen1827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1828" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not in dark speeches--</hi>parables or similitudes.<div eID="gen1828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1829" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the similitude of the Lord shall he behold--</hi>not the face or essence of God, who is invisible (<reference osisRef="Exod.33.20">Ex 33:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.15">Col 1:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.1.18">Joh 1:18</reference>); but some unmistakable evidence of His glorious presence (<reference osisRef="Exod.33.2">Ex 33:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.34.5">34:5</reference>). The latter clause should have been conjoined with the preceding one, thus: "not in dark speeches, and in a figure shall he behold the Lord." The slight change in the punctuation removes all appearance of contradiction to <reference osisRef="Deut.4.15">De 4:15</reference>. <div eID="gen1829" type="x-p"/>

Miriam's Leprosy.</title> <div sID="gen1830" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1355"/><hi type="bold">10. the cloud departed from the tabernacle--</hi>that is, from the door to resume its permanent position over the mercy seat.<div eID="gen1830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1831" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Miriam became leprous--</hi>This malady in its most malignant form (<reference osisRef="Exod.4.6">Ex 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.27">2Ki 5:27</reference>) as its color, combined with its sudden appearance, proved, was inflicted as a divine judgment; and she was made the victim, either because of her extreme violence or because the leprosy on Aaron would have interrupted or dishonored the holy service. <div eID="gen1831" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain:
Nu 12:10-16. Miriam's Leprosy.

10. the cloud departed from the tabernacle--that is, from the door to resume its permanent position over the mercy seat.
 
Miriam became leprous--This malady in its most malignant form (Ex 4:6; 2Ki 5:27) as its color, combined with its sudden appearance, proved, was inflicted as a divine judgment; and she was made the victim, either because of her extreme violence or because the leprosy on Aaron would have interrupted or dishonored the holy service.
